processing: As with other Mengku raw pu-erh, the leaf is pan-fired, rolled and sun-dried, then pressed or kept loose. Lahu growers' own processing was long considered uneven, which held its price back.
harvest_season: Spring is the most valued picking, as is usual across Mengku.
appearance_dry: Long dark green strips of large leaf, typical of Mengku raw tea.
appearance_wet: Thick yellow-green large leaves that open fully.
taste_profile: Little is recorded about this village's own taste. As with other Mengku raw teas, expect a full body, some bitterness and a returning sweetness.

brewing.notes: Hot water and short early steeps, as with other young Mengku raw teas; lengthen only once the bitterness has settled.

vintage_note: Sold by harvest year as mao cha or pressed cakes, usually under the Bingdao name with the village added. One spring list priced old-tree Nanpo at 4,500 to 4,800 yuan a kilo, the highest of the Bingdao villages it listed after the old village. Ask for the village and tree age in writing, since blending inside the Bingdao area is common.
description:
Nanpo is a Lahu village in the Bingdao village committee, on the western side of the Nanmeng River in Mengku. It has one of the larger stretches of old garden in the Bingdao group, spread through the forest around the old settlement.

The tea is made in the usual raw pu-erh way from Mengku large-leaf. For a long time its reputation suffered from rough local processing rather than from the leaf, and a good maker matters a lot here.

Flavour notes specific to Nanpo are scarce. As with other Mengku raw teas, expect thickness, some bitterness and returning sweetness. Use hot water and short steeps at first.

Prices sit between the old village and the cheaper Bingdao settlements on one published price list, which makes it an interesting middle step when tasting through the five villages. Buy from sellers who name the maker and the year.
history:
Nanpo's old village once had more than 70 households. Because of its height and poor roads, Shuangjiang County decided in 2000 to move it down to the highway below Bingdao, though more than ten families later returned to their fields, walnut trees and tea gardens.

Hundreds of acres of old gardens are reported around the old village. One regional account puts the village's age at no less than 500 years, an estimate rather than a documented date.
